summary: Learners measure the volume of a solid by counting the unit cubes that fill it and recording the result in the matching cubic unit (cm³, in³, ft³). The key skill is organising the count: structure the array into rows, columns and especially layers, count one layer and iterate it for the number of layers, account for cubes hidden from view (and, in larger solids, fully interior cubes), and avoid double-counting shared edges and corners. Correct cubic-unit notation (cm³, not cm²) is part of the objective. Filling real containers with cubes grounds the method before relying on diagrams.
misconceptions: Counts only visible cubes and misses hidden interior cubes (Strategy C).
Double-counts cubes on shared edges and corners.
Records volume in square units (cm²) instead of cubic units (cm³).

activities.title: Fill a box and count by layers
steps: Fill a small open box (or transparent container) whose inside length, width and height are whole numbers of centimetres with centimetre cubes so they pack in snugly, leaving no gaps.
Find the number of cubes in the bottom layer (for a 4 by 3 base, count 4×3 = 12).
Count how many identical layers stack to fill the box (e.g. 2 layers), then add 12 for each layer: 12, 24.
Write the volume with its unit: 24 cm³. State explicitly why it is cm³ and not cm².
Predict the count before filling, then check by filling; investigate any mismatch to find double-counted or missed cubes.
activities.insight: Measuring volume means counting all the unit cubes that fill the solid. Organising them into layers (one layer multiplied by the number of layers) is more reliable and efficient than counting one-by-one, and counting only the visible faces misses hidden cubes. The unit is 'cubes', so it is recorded in cubic units.

activities.title: Count the hidden cubes in a drawing
steps: Study an isometric drawing of a cuboid built from centimetre cubes (e.g. 4 by 3 by 2).

Identify which cubes are occluded from this single view (at the back and underneath) that the drawing does not show directly, and describe how you know they are there; note that larger solids also contain fully interior cubes a view cannot show.
Count by layers: state the cubes in one layer, then multiply or add across the number of layers to reach the total.
Shade or mark each layer as you count it so no cube is counted twice on a shared edge or corner.
Record the total with the correct cubic unit and explain your reasoning.
activities.insight: A flat drawing of a solid hides cubes at the back and underneath (and fully interior cubes in larger solids); a reliable count reconstructs the full array by layers rather than tallying the cubes visible on the faces.

activities.title: Cubic units versus square units
steps: Given several measured counts, write each volume with the correct cubic unit (cm³, in³, ft³) to match the cube used.
Explain the difference between cm² (area, covering a flat surface with squares) and cm³ (volume, filling a space with cubes).
Spot and correct deliberately mislabelled answers such as '24 cm²' for a volume.
Describe in words why volume is measured in cubic units.
activities.insight: Volume is counted in unit cubes, so it is recorded in cubic units; this notation is distinct from the square units used for area.

checkQuestion: Give the child an isometric diagram of a cuboid built from centimetre cubes (4 by 3 by 2) and a small open box with a bag of centimetre cubes. Say: 'Find the volume of the drawn solid by counting its unit cubes, then measure the volume of this box by filling it — and write each answer with its unit.' Then WATCH how they count (cube-by-cube versus by layers), whether they account for hidden cubes and avoid double-counting, and whether they write cm³.
checkAnswer: Counts 24 cubic units for the diagram by structuring into layers (a 4×3 layer of 12, two layers = 24), accounts for hidden cubes without double-counting, fills the box systematically, and records both volumes in cm³.
